title: Boss: where did my data go?
summary: Three data and network tickets on a real Docker Engine: mounts done right, three tiers wired, a clean-up that keeps the data.

steps.title: Post-incident questions
body: Data and networking tickets are where Docker surprises people: a site that a container could overwrite, a web tier
that can talk straight to the database, a clean-up that took the data with it. Each ticket below opens its own
machine with a **real Docker Engine**. Use `--mount`, `docker network`, `docker volume` and `docker inspect -f`.

steps.title: Ticket 1: serve a folder, read-only
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal. Serve `~/site` with a container named `web` (`busybox:1.37` running
`httpd -f -p 80 -h /www`), published on host port `8080`, so that:
1. `~/site` is mounted at `/www` **read-only**, written with the long `--mount` syntax;
2. `/tmp` in the container is a **tmpfs** (in memory, gone when the container stops);
3. `curl http://localhost:8080/` shows the page, and an edit to `~/site/index.html` shows up without restarting.

checks.name: ~/site is bind-mounted read-only at /www
checks.fail: `/www` is not a read-only bind mount of `~/site`. `--mount type=bind,source=$HOME/site,target=/www,readonly`.

checks.name: /tmp is a tmpfs
checks.fail: `/tmp` is not a tmpfs mount. `--mount type=tmpfs,target=/tmp`.

checks.name: the container cannot write the site
checks.fail: The container can write into `/www`: mount it read-only.

checks.name: it was written with --mount
checks.fail: Use the long `--mount type=bind,...` syntax for the site (it records the mount under `HostConfig.Mounts`).

hints: `--mount` takes comma-separated `key=value` pairs: `type`, `source`, `target`, plus the bare flag `readonly`.
`--mount` needs an absolute source path: `source=$HOME/site` (the shell expands `$HOME`).
solution: docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 --mount type=bind,source=$HOME/site,target=/www,readonly --mount type=tmpfs,target=/tmp busybox:1.37 httpd -f -p 80 -h /www
steps.explain: `--mount` spells out what `-v` leaves implicit, and fails loudly where `-v` would silently create an empty folder for a mistyped path. Read-only mounts are a cheap security control: a compromised web server cannot deface what it serves. tmpfs gives scratch space that never reaches the disk, which also suits `--read-only` containers.

steps.title: Ticket 2: wire three tiers
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal with `web` (published on port 8080), `api` (HTTP on port 5000) and `db`
(PostgreSQL-like on 5432), all on the default bridge. Wire them like production, keeping the same containers:
1. `web` reaches `api` by name: `docker exec web wget -qO- http://api:5000/` prints `api 1.0`;
2. `api` reaches `db` by name: `docker exec api nc -w 2 db 5432` prints `PostgreSQL 17 ready`;
3. `web` cannot reach `db` in any way, and nothing but `api` shares a network with `db`;
4. `curl http://localhost:8080/` still answers `web 1.0` from this machine.

checks.name: web cannot reach db
checks.cmd: for ip in $(docker inspect -f '{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}} {{end}}' db) db; do if docker exec web nc -w 2 $ip 5432 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep -q ready; then echo "web reached db at $ip"; exit 1; fi; done
checks.fail: `web` can still reach `db`. Keep `db` off every network `web` is on (the default bridge included).

checks.name: db shares a network with api only
checks.cmd: for n in $(docker inspect -f '{{range $n, $_ := .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{$n}} {{end}}' db); do docker network inspect -f '{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}' $n; done | sort -u | xargs
checks.fail: Something other than `api` and `db` shares a network with `db`.

hints: `docker network create front` and `docker network create back`; a container can be on several networks.
`api` joins both; `web` joins `front`; `db` joins `back` and leaves `bridge`.
Published ports keep working when a container leaves the default bridge, as long as it is on some bridge network.
steps.explain: Networks are Docker's security boundary between containers: a container can only reach networks it is attached to, so the database on `back` is invisible to the web tier on `front`, and `api` is the one bridge between them. Compose builds exactly this with `networks:` per service.

steps.title: Ticket 3: clean up, keep the data
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal. The dev box is full: `docker ps -a`, `docker volume ls`,
1. remove every **stopped** container (the retired `old-db` included); `web` keeps running;
2. remove the **anonymous** volumes nobody uses any more;
3. keep the named volumes `pgdata` (the retired database's data, needed for a migration) and `reports`, with their

checks.name: no stopped containers are left, web still runs
checks.cmd: test -z "$(docker ps -aq --filter status=exited --filter status=created)" && test "$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Running}}' web)" = true
checks.fail: There are still stopped containers (`docker ps -a --filter status=exited`), or `web` was removed.

checks.name: no anonymous volumes are left
checks.fail: Anonymous volumes (the 64-hex names) are still there. `docker volume prune` removes unused anonymous volumes.

checks.name: pgdata and reports kept their data
checks.cmd: docker run --rm -v pgdata:/p -v reports:/r busybox:1.37 cat /p/base.txt /r/q3.txt
checks.fail: `pgdata` or `reports` is gone or empty. Since Docker 23, `docker volume prune` keeps named volumes; `docker volume prune -a` (and `docker system prune --volumes -a`) delete them.

hints: `docker container prune -f` removes every stopped container; `docker rm` does not remove a container's volumes unless you add `-v`.
`docker volume ls -f dangling=true` lists volumes no container uses; anonymous ones have 64-hex names.
`docker volume prune -f` (no `-a`) removes only anonymous unused volumes.
steps.explain: Containers, images, volumes and build cache are cleaned separately, and volumes are the dangerous one: they hold data. Since Docker 23 `docker volume prune` only removes anonymous volumes; adding `-a` (or `docker system prune -a --volumes`) also deletes named ones, which is how people lose a database on a Friday. `docker system df` shows where the space went before you delete anything.
